regional.incubation: Decades. Myelopathy appears after years; leukaemia typically forty to sixty years after perinatal infection.
regional.syndrome: Lifelong asymptomatic carriage in over 90%. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) appears after a latency of forty to sixty years, usually in those infected through breastfeeding, with a lifetime risk of a few per cent; HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) in under 4%, presenting as spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Also infective dermatitis of childhood, uveitis, and Strongyloides hyperinfection, the last because the virus distorts the Th2 response that normally contains the worm.
regional.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.
regional.prevention: Avoiding breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist, which is what cut transmission in Nagasaki; leucodepletion and donor screening of blood; condoms; not sharing injecting equipment. No vaccine.
regional.geography: Sharply defined endemic foci rather than a global distribution: south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, West and Central Africa, Iran, Romania, and Aboriginal communities of central Australia, where some adult seroprevalences exceed 40%.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

Secondary infection with a different serotype raises severe-disease risk through antibody-dependent enhancement.
